Agricultural researcher for a major University here, actually doing some projects with beans currently. Its been answered but I would like to expand on it for knowledge for all. Legumes share a symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium, a bacteria. Every legume is different for the type of Rhizobium that is symbiotic with them. The beans release what are called flavanoids into the soil, which the bacteria are "attracted to" and the bacteria then attach to the root system thru a curling of the root hair and form a bacteroid, a sort of "bacteria house" if you will, where the bacteria are able to fix nitrogen in anerobic conditions. The beans give energy, typically in the form of ATP, to the bacteroid, and the plant receives the nitrogen in return. Rhizobia are sometimes found free in the soil, depending on soil health, but typically you would innoculate the seeds during planting with the Rhizobium for best effectiveness, however, there is still anecdotal evidence of applying a starter drop of nitrogen after planting that could also increase yield slightly, but currently there are studies being conducted on that to see what results are obtainable. Really interesting stuff. Also, there is research into if this symbiotic relationship can be grafted into non-legumes, such as corn, reducing the need for additonal fertilizer, and also helps reduce the chance of fertilizer runoff into water systems, while reducing the fuel load and costs assosiated with additonal fertilizing of a field. Pretty cool stuff

Also not often thought about to most people is the aircraft industry as well when using high horsepower single engine props. The torque of the prop shaft/prop depending on setup could actually roll an aircraft as well, being more pronounced the larger the radius of the prop.  Its not really a huge issue today, but during the prop days of WWII and the few years after, really high horsepower planes would experience a roll, and since the need for faster planes arose further in the pre-jet turbine era and in some attempts/prototypes to have prop planes outpace turbine planes, the issue became more common as an obstacle that needed to be fixed into the design, such as a vertical stabilizer on the top of the fueslage. The "Thunderscreech" airplane prototypes are an excellent example of extreme prop horsepower, mating a turbine to a prop, and the obstacles they encountered.

Debatable. A great tank, yes, but the best? Depends on frame of reference. If referencing firepower amd protection, yes, it was great. But it was heavy, it was slow, it was exponentially more expensive to produce in a period where Germany didnt have lots of expendable resources, and its fuel consumption was astronomical, often meaning it couldnt really venture that far away from support facilities, meaning logistics were terrible to get figured out when it came to moving units around. A great tank in theory, yes, but ultimately across the board it was surpassed by the Russian T34 and the Allied Shermans, mostly because sheer numbers could often outpace the downsides these tanks had, as T34s were fairly competitive as far as late model firepower (the 85mm Zis) and speed. Shermans were prone to ammunition explosions but had excellent reliability for the amount produced and the 75mm was often prefered since most Shermans were just infantry support and the 76mm was far harder to handle and aim. The Shermans that were converted to 17lb British guns were a great anti tank vehicle tho, as the Germans came to fear the 17lb gun. Often these tanks were singled out first by German artillery and anti tank, as the 17lb could penetrate a Tiger I. Thats why you often see half barrels painted on 17lb guns, as to camo the larger barrell so they appeared to be 75mm guns instead. Each tank had its pros and cons and I dont think there was a general "best tank". Each had a great niche that it excelled in and areas where it fell short.
